source_text: Anyone who compares a field of cultivated wheat with a stand of wild grass will notice the same thing: the crop plants vary more among themselves than the wild ones do. The same holds for livestock. Two dairy cows from the same herd can differ in size, color, temperament, and yield far more than two deer from the same forest. This is not a coincidence, and it is not simply the result of breeders picking out odd individuals. It seems to come from the conditions under which domesticated species live. A wild population faces a fairly stable set of pressures over long stretches of time. A cultivated one is moved between climates, fed on new diets, sheltered from predators, and bred in ways that would never happen on its own. Those changes in circumstance appear to loosen whatever holds a species to its typical form. Some researchers have suggested that a rich food supply plays a particular role, and that seems plausible, though it is hard to separate from everything else that changes when an animal is brought under human care. What is clearer is that the effect takes time to appear and does not readily switch off. A species may need to live for several generations under new conditions before it starts producing noticeable variants, but once it does, it tends to keep producing them. Even our oldest crops continue to throw off new strains, and our oldest domestic animals are still being reshaped by breeders today.
output_text:
Cultivated plants and domestic animals vary among themselves more than wild ones do. The plants in a field of cultivated wheat differ from one another more than the plants in a stand of wild grass, and two dairy cows from one herd can be far less alike in size, color, temperament, and yield than two deer from one forest.

This is no coincidence, and breeders who pick out the odd individuals are not the whole reason for it. The reason seems to lie in how domesticated species live. A wild population spends long stretches of time under pressures that stay fairly stable. We carry a cultivated one from one climate to another, feed it things it never ate before, keep predators away from it, and breed it in ways that would never come about without us. All of that change appears to weaken whatever it is that keeps a species to its typical form. Some researchers have suggested that a rich food supply plays a particular part. That seems plausible, but food is only one of the things that change when an animal is taken into human care, and its effect is hard to separate from the rest.

The timing is less in doubt. Noticeable variants may not appear until a species has spent several generations under new conditions. Once they have begun to appear, they tend to keep coming. The crops we have grown longest are still producing new strains, and breeders are still reshaping the animals we have kept longest.
notes: The draft credits the food-supply idea to "some researchers" without naming them, and nothing in it identifies them, so the attribution stays as written. If you have the source, name it in that sentence.

source_text: I was born on a small farm outside a market town in eastern Maryland. I cannot say exactly when. No one wrote it down, or if they did, I never saw the record. That was the ordinary situation for enslaved people in that part of the country. Most of them could not have told you the year of their birth, let alone the day, and the men who owned them preferred it that way. Dates were kept for livestock and account books, not for people who were themselves entered in the account book. When someone did try to place a birth, they used the seasons: around planting, around harvest, the year the cherries came in early. As a child this bothered me more than I could explain. The white children knew how old they were and said so freely. I did not understand what made my case different, and I was not permitted to ask. My owner treated any question of that kind as a sign of insolence, the first symptom of a slave who was thinking too much. My best guess now is that I am in my late twenties. I arrived at that figure only because I once overheard him mention my age in passing, and I have been counting forward from it ever since.
output_text:
I can name the place of my birth, a small farm outside a market town in eastern Maryland, but not exactly the date. Either nobody wrote it down, or somebody did and I never saw the record.

Among enslaved people in that part of the country this was ordinary. Most could not have named the year they were born, much less the day, and that was how the men who owned them preferred it. Owners kept dates for their livestock and their account books, and kept none for the people who were themselves written into those books. A birth, if anyone tried to place it at all, was placed by the season: around planting, around harvest, the year the cherries came in early.

As a child I felt the lack more than I could explain. The white children knew their ages and spoke of them freely, and I could not understand what set my case apart from theirs. Asking was not permitted. To my owner any question of the kind was insolence, the first symptom that a slave had been thinking too much.

I put myself now in my late twenties. That is my best guess, and I can make it only because I once overheard him mention my age in passing and have counted forward from that number ever since.

source_text: Since I have mentioned my father, it seems worth saying a little about what he was like. He was physically sound, of average height but solidly built and unusually strong. He had a range of small talents that he never made much of: he could sketch well, knew enough music to play a few hymns on the fiddle, and had a good singing voice, so that on evenings when the shop was closed he would sometimes play and sing for the family, which we all enjoyed. He was also handy in a general way and could pick up almost any tradesman's tools and use them competently. But the thing people valued most in him was his judgment. He had a practical, level-headed way of thinking about problems, whether they were domestic or public, and neighbors came to rely on it. He never held any office; with a large family to support and not much money, he could not afford time away from his trade. Even so, I remember prominent men from the town and from his congregation calling at the house to ask his view on some matter under discussion, and listening to his answer with real attention. Private individuals brought him their disputes too, and he was often asked to arbitrate between parties who could not settle a quarrel on their own.
output_text:
My father was of average height, but he was solidly built, sound in body, and unusually strong. He could sketch well, he had a good singing voice, and he knew enough music to manage a few hymns on the fiddle, though he never made much of these small talents. On some evenings when the shop was closed he would play and sing for the family, which pleased us all. Handy in a general way, he was competent with almost any tradesman's tools once he had them in hand.

But people valued him most for his judgment. On a problem, whether domestic or public, he thought practically and kept a level head, and his neighbors came to rely on him for it. He never held an office. A large family to support and little money made time away from his trade more than he could afford. All the same, I remember prominent men of the town and of his congregation coming to the house to ask what he thought of some matter then under discussion, and attending closely to his answer. Private persons brought him their disputes as well, and when the parties to a quarrel could not settle it themselves, he was often asked to arbitrate.

source_text: The simplest way to understand what government is for is to imagine a situation without one. Picture a handful of people who have landed in some remote place, cut off from every other society. They stand in for the first inhabitants of any country. The first thing they will do, before anyone thinks about rules or leaders, is form a community, because none of them can manage alone. One person's needs run far ahead of one person's strength, and few people can stand extended isolation. Each of them will look for help from the others, and each will be asked for help in return. Consider the practical problem of building shelter. Four or five people working together can put up a decent cabin in a clearing within a season. A single person could spend an entire lifetime and never finish. He might cut down the trees, but he could not haul the logs, and if he somehow hauled them, he could not raise them into walls by himself. In the meantime he has to eat, so every day the work is interrupted by hunting or gathering, and every new need drags him off in another direction. If he falls ill or breaks a leg, he is finished, not because the injury itself would kill him but because it would stop him from doing the work that keeps him alive.
output_text:
The purpose of government is easiest to see by imagining a place without one. Suppose a handful of people have landed somewhere remote, out of reach of any other society, and let them stand for the first inhabitants of any country. Not one of them can manage alone. A single person needs far more than a single person's strength can supply, and few people can bear isolation for long. So they will form a community first, before any of them gives a thought to rules or leaders. Each will turn to the others for help and be asked for help in turn.

Take the building of a shelter. Working together, four or five of them can have a decent cabin standing in a clearing within a season, while one person alone could give his whole life to the job and never finish it. Felling the trees may be within his power. Hauling the logs is not, and if he somehow got them hauled, lifting them into walls would still take more than one man. All the while he has to eat, so hunting or gathering breaks into the work every day, and each new need pulls him off somewhere else. Should he fall ill or break a leg, he is finished. The injury itself need not kill him, but it would stop the work that keeps him alive.

source_text: Most of us worry far more than our circumstances require. We could hand off a good share of the care we lavish on ourselves and lose nothing by it, since the world is built to accommodate our weak points as well as our strong ones. For some people, constant anxiety has become a chronic condition that no amount of reassurance seems to cure. Part of the problem is that we overrate the importance of our own work. Look at how much gets done without us, and think about what would happen if we were laid up for a month: things would mostly carry on. Yet we stay on guard all day, refusing to trust anything we cannot control, and only at night, worn out, do we reluctantly let go and accept that the next day is uncertain. We are so committed to living the way we live that we treat our habits as sacred and cannot imagine doing otherwise. This is the only way, we tell ourselves. But there are as many ways to live as there are directions to walk from a single point. Change looks like a miracle from the outside, and yet it is happening all the time, in small increments, to everyone. Real knowledge, as an old proverb puts it, is knowing what you know and knowing what you do not. And once one person has turned a hope into a fact, sooner or later everyone builds on it.
output_text:
A great deal gets done without us, and if any one of us were laid up for a month, most things would go on as before. We overrate the importance of our own work, and that is part of why most of us carry far more worry than our circumstances call for. A good share of the care we lavish on ourselves is care we could hand off and never miss, because the world is made to fit our weaknesses as well as our strengths. Still we stand guard all day and trust nothing we cannot control. By night we are worn out, and only then, reluctantly, do we let go and accept that tomorrow is uncertain. In some people the anxiety never stops. It has become chronic, and no amount of reassurance seems to cure it.

We are so set on living as we do that we hold our habits sacred and cannot picture living any other way. We tell ourselves that this is the only way, when the ways to live are as many as the directions a person can walk from one point. Seen from outside, change looks like a miracle, but it is happening to everyone, continually and by small steps. An old proverb says that real knowledge is knowing what you know and knowing what you do not. A hope that one person has made into a fact becomes, sooner or later, something everyone builds on.
notes: The draft's last three claims (change is constant, the proverb about knowledge, one person's hope becoming a fact everyone builds on) have no stated link to each other or to the argument about worry, so they stand as separate claims in the draft's order. The proverb is also unidentified; add the connection or the source if you have them.

source_text: By the time I could read the river the way I could read a page, and knew every bend and snag and sandbar along it by heart, I had gained a skill that would earn me a living. But the skill came at a cost, and the cost was permanent. The river stopped being beautiful to me. I can still remember a particular sunset from my first weeks on the water, before any of that had happened. The whole surface of the river had gone red, fading to gold in the middle distance, and a single dark log drifted through the gold like a stroke of ink. Off to one side a long slanting streak caught the light and sparkled. Somewhere else the water churned in slow rings that shifted through every color you could name. Where the red was palest there was a patch of glassy water marked with faint circles and radiating lines, as if someone had drawn them with a fine pen. The left bank was heavy forest, and the shadow it threw across the water was cut in one place by a bright ruffled path that looked like beaten silver. Above the treeline a dead tree with a single living branch stood against the sky, and that branch caught the last full light of the sun and seemed to burn. There were curves and reflections, wooded bluffs, softened distances, and over all of it the light kept shifting as the sun went down, so that every minute the scene rearranged itself into something new. I had never seen anything like it, and at the time I did not know that I was looking at it for the last time in that way.
output_text:
I learned to read the river as I would read a page, until I knew every bend, snag, and sandbar along it by heart. That skill would earn me a living, but it cost me the beauty of the river, and the loss was permanent.

None of this had happened yet in my first weeks on the water, and one sunset from those weeks has stayed with me. The river's whole surface had turned red, and the red shaded into gold in the middle distance, where one dark log drifted across the gold like a stroke of ink. A long, slanting streak sparkled in the light off to one side, and in another place the water churned in slow rings that passed through every color that has a name. The palest part of the red held a patch of water smooth as glass, and on it were faint circles and radiating lines that might have been drawn with a fine pen. Heavy forest covered the left bank and threw a shadow over the water, broken in one place by a bright, ruffled path with the look of beaten silver. Above the treeline a dead tree stood against the sky. It had one living branch, which took the last full light of the sun and seemed to burn. There were curves, reflections, wooded bluffs, and distances gone soft, and as the sun went down the light over all of them kept shifting, so that the scene remade itself into something new every minute. I had seen nothing like it before, and I did not know then that I would not see it that way again.

source_text: The study of variation in domesticated species is a topic of great importance to anyone interested in the natural world. When we look to the individuals of the same variety or sub-variety of our older cultivated plants and animals, one of the first points which strikes us, is, that they generally differ much more from each other, than do the individuals of any one species or variety in a state of nature. When we reflect on the vast diversity of the plants and animals which have been cultivated, and which have varied during all ages under the most different climates and treatment, I think we are fundamentally driven to conclude that this greater variability is simply due to our domestic productions having been raised under conditions of life not so uniform as, and somewhat different from, those to which the parent-species have been exposed under nature. There is, also, I think, some probability in the view propounded by Andrew Knight, that this variability may be partly connected with excess of food. It seems pretty clear that organic beings must be exposed during several generations to the new conditions of life in order to cause any appreciable amount of variation; and that when the organisation has once begun to vary, it generally continues to vary for many generations. No case is on record of a variable being ceasing to be variable under cultivation, underscoring the enduring importance of this phenomenon. Our oldest cultivated plants, such as wheat, still often yield new varieties: our oldest domesticated animals are still capable of rapid improvement or modification. Ultimately, these observations remind us that nature is always full of surprises, and there is always more to learn.
output_text:
Within a single variety or sub-variety of our older cultivated plants and animals, individuals generally differ from each other much more than the individuals of any one species or variety do in a state of nature. Few points strike us sooner when we look at these plants and animals.

The plants and animals we have cultivated are vastly diverse, and they have varied in every age, in the most different climates and under the most different treatment. When we reflect on that, I think the conclusion is forced on us that their greater variability is due simply to the conditions of life under which they have been raised. Those conditions have been less uniform than the ones the parent-species were exposed to under nature, and somewhat different from them. Andrew Knight put forward the view that this variability may be connected in part with excess of food, and I think his view has some probability as well.

Organic beings must, it seems fairly clear, live under the new conditions of life for several generations before those conditions cause any appreciable variation. It seems just as clear that organic beings which have once begun to vary generally go on varying for many generations. No variable being is on record as having ceased to vary under cultivation. The plants we have cultivated longest, wheat among them, still often yield new varieties, and the animals we domesticated earliest can still be improved or modified rapidly.
notes:
Origin note: this draft's origin was not stated, so it was fully recomposed. If you wrote it, say so and the next run keeps your wording.

Three claims were left out because the draft gives them no support: that the study of this variation is of great importance, that the lack of any recorded exception underscores the "enduring importance of this phenomenon", and the closing lesson that nature is always full of surprises. Each needs a stated consequence or evidence before it can go back in.

source_text: Knowing where and when you were born is one of the most basic and important facts about a person's life. I was born in Tuckahoe, near Hillsborough, and about twelve miles from Easton, in Talbot county, Maryland. I have no accurate knowledge of my age, never having seen any authentic record containing it. By far the larger part of the slaves know as little of their ages as horses know of theirs, and it is the wish of most masters within my knowledge to keep their slaves thus fundamentally ignorant. I do not remember to have ever met a slave who could tell of his birthday. They seldom come nearer to it than planting-time, harvest-time, cherry-time, spring-time, or fall-time. A want of information concerning my own was a source of unhappiness to me even during childhood. The white children could tell their ages, highlighting the stark inequality of the situation. I could not tell why I ought to be deprived of the same privilege. I was not allowed, it is important to note, to make any inquiries of my master concerning it. He deemed all such inquiries on the part of a slave improper and impertinent, and evidence of a restless spirit. The nearest estimate I can give makes me now between twenty-seven and twenty-eight years of age. I come to this, from hearing my master say, some time during 1835, I was about seventeen years old. In the end, this experience taught me that knowledge is a gift no one should ever take for granted.
output_text:
Tuckahoe, where I was born, lies near Hillsborough and about twelve miles from Easton, in Talbot county, Maryland. I have never seen any authentic record of my age, and I do not know it accurately. As nearly as I can estimate, I am now between twenty-seven and twenty-eight years of age. The figure comes from a remark of my master's, made in my hearing some time during 1835, that I was about seventeen years old.

The great majority of slaves know no more about their ages than horses know about theirs, and most of the masters I know of want to keep their slaves in that ignorance. Of all the slaves I have met, I cannot recall one who could tell his birthday. The nearest they usually come to it is planting-time, harvest-time, cherry-time, spring-time, or fall-time.

Not knowing my own birthday made me unhappy even as a child. The white children could say how old they were, and I could not see why the same privilege should be kept from me. I was not allowed to ask my master anything about it. In his view, any such question from a slave was improper and impertinent, and a sign of a restless spirit.
notes:
Origin note: this draft's origin was not stated, so it was fully recomposed. If you wrote it, say so and the next run keeps your wording.

Three general verdicts were left out because the draft states them without evidence or consequence: the opening line that knowing where and when you were born is one of the most basic and important facts of a life, the "stark inequality" label, and the closing lesson that knowledge is a gift no one should take for granted. The facts under them are all still in the piece.

source_text: Family history is an important subject, and few figures matter more in anyone's story than a parent. I think you may like to know something of his person and character. He had an excellent constitution of body, was of middle stature, but well set, and very strong; he was ingenious, could draw prettily, was skilled a little in music, and had a clear pleasing voice, so that when he played psalm tunes on his violin and sung withal, as he sometimes did in an evening after the business of the day was over, it was extremely agreeable to hear. He had a mechanical genius too, and, on occasion, was very handy in the use of other tradesmen's tools; but his great excellence fundamentally lay in a sound understanding and solid judgment in prudential matters, both in private and publick affairs. In the latter, indeed, he was never employed, the numerous family he had to educate and the straitness of his circumstances keeping him close to his trade; but I remember well his being frequently visited by leading people, who consulted him for his opinion in affairs of the town or of the church he belonged to, and showed a good deal of respect for his judgment and advice: he was also, it is worth noting, much consulted by private persons about their affairs when any difficulty occurred, and frequently chosen an arbitrator between contending parties, demonstrating the deep trust the community placed in him. His example is a reminder that true character, not status, is what ultimately earns the respect of others.
output_text:
I think you may like to hear what he was like, in body and in character. He was a man of middle height, but well set and very strong, with an excellent constitution. He was ingenious, could draw prettily, and had a little skill in music. His voice was clear and pleasing, which made it extremely agreeable to listen when he played psalm tunes on his violin and sang along, as he sometimes did in the evening once the day's business was over.

He also had a genius for mechanical work, and on occasion he was very handy with other tradesmen's tools. His great excellence, though, was a sound understanding and solid judgment in matters of prudence, private and public alike. It is true that he was never employed in public affairs, since the large family he had to educate and his straitened circumstances kept him close to his trade. But I well remember how often leading people came to see him. They asked his opinion on the affairs of the town or of his church, and they treated his judgment and advice with a good deal of respect. Private persons consulted him a great deal too, whenever some difficulty arose in their affairs, and he was frequently chosen to arbitrate between contending parties.
notes:
Origin note: this draft's origin was not stated, so it was fully recomposed. If you wrote it, say so and the next run keeps your wording.

Open question: the draft never says who "he" is. Its opening line implies a parent of the writer but nothing states it, so the piece keeps "he" and does not call him "my father"; name him if that is right.

Three general verdicts were left out because the draft states them without evidence or consequence: the opening line that family history is important and few figures matter more than a parent, the gloss about "the deep trust the community placed in him", and the closing moral that true character, not status, earns respect.

source_text: The question of why governments exist is one of the most important questions in political thought. In order to gain a clear and just idea of the design and end of government, let us suppose a small number of persons settled in some sequestered part of the earth, unconnected with the rest, they will then represent the first peopling of any country, or of the world. In this state of natural liberty, society will be their first thought, highlighting the importance of community to human survival. A thousand motives will excite them thereto, the strength of one man is so fundamentally unequal to his wants, and his mind so unfitted for perpetual solitude, that he is soon obliged to seek assistance and relief of another, who in his turn requires the same. Four or five united, it is important to note, would be able to raise a tolerable dwelling in the midst of a wilderness, but one man might labour out of the common period of life without accomplishing any thing; when he had felled his timber he could not remove it, nor erect it after it was removed; hunger in the mean time would urge him from his work, and every different want call him a different way. Disease, nay even misfortune would be death, for though neither might be mortal, yet either would disable him from living, and reduce him to a state in which he might rather be said to perish than to die. This simple story shows that cooperation is the foundation of every society, and it is a lesson worth remembering today.
output_text:
To see clearly and justly what government is designed for and what end it serves, suppose a small number of people settled in some secluded part of the earth, with no connection to the rest. They will then stand for the first people of any country, or of the world.

In that state of natural liberty, the first thing they will think of is society. A thousand motives will push them toward it. One man's strength falls so far short of his wants, and his mind is so ill suited to permanent solitude, that he soon has to look to another for help and relief, and the other needs the same in his turn. Four or five together could put up a tolerable dwelling in the middle of a wilderness, while one man might work through the ordinary span of a life and accomplish nothing. He could fell his timber but not move it, and once it was moved he could not raise it. Hunger would meanwhile drive him from the work, and each separate want would pull him a separate way. Disease would be death to him, and even misfortune would, since either one, though it might not be mortal, would leave him unable to live, in a condition where he might more truly be said to perish than to die.
notes:
Origin note: this draft's origin was not stated, so it was fully recomposed. If you wrote it, say so and the next run keeps your wording.

Three general verdicts were left out because the draft states them without evidence or consequence: the opening claim that why governments exist is one of the most important questions in political thought, the remark on "the importance of community to human survival", and the closing lesson that cooperation is the foundation of every society.

I read "labour out of the common period of life" as working through a whole ordinary lifetime; change that sentence if you meant working beyond one.

source_text: Anxiety and trust are important themes that affect every aspect of how we live our lives. I think that we may safely trust a good deal more than we do. We may waive just so much care of ourselves as we honestly bestow elsewhere. Nature, it is important to note, is as well adapted to our weakness as to our strength. The incessant anxiety and strain of some is a well nigh incurable form of disease, underscoring the importance of mental well-being. We are made to significantly exaggerate the importance of what work we do; and yet how much is not done by us! or, what if we had been taken sick? How vigilant we are! determined not to live by faith if we can avoid it; all the day long on the alert, at night we unwillingly say our prayers and commit ourselves to uncertainties. So thoroughly and sincerely are we compelled to live, reverencing our life, and denying the possibility of change. This is the only way, we say; but there are as many ways as there can be drawn radii from one centre. All change is a miracle to contemplate; but it is a miracle which is taking place every instant. Confucius said, “To know that we know what we know, and that we do not know what we do not know, that is true knowledge.” When one man has reduced a fact of the imagination to be a fact to his understanding, I foresee that all men at length establish their lives on that basis. If we can learn to let go of our worries, we can all live fuller and more meaningful lives.
output_text:
I think our trust may safely go a good deal further than it does. The care we honestly give elsewhere is care we may stop taking of ourselves, in just that measure. Nature suits our weakness as well as it suits our strength. In some people the anxiety and strain never stop, and that is a form of disease almost beyond cure.

We are made to overrate the importance of whatever work we do. Yet how much is done that is none of our doing! Or had we fallen sick, what then? We keep such watch, resolved not to live by faith if we can help it. All day we stay on guard, and at night we say our prayers unwillingly and hand ourselves over to uncertainties. That is how thoroughly and sincerely we are compelled to live, revering our life and denying that change is possible.

We say there is no other way, but the ways are as many as the radii that can be drawn from one centre. Contemplate any change and it is a miracle, though one that is happening every instant. Confucius said, “To know that we know what we know, and that we do not know what we do not know, that is true knowledge.” Once one man has turned a fact of the imagination into a fact for his understanding, I foresee all men in time founding their lives on it.
notes:
Origin note: this draft's origin was not stated, so it was fully recomposed. If you wrote it, say so and the next run keeps your wording.

Three general verdicts were left out because the draft states them without evidence or consequence: the opening line that anxiety and trust are important themes affecting every aspect of life, the remark on "the importance of mental well-being", and the closing promise that letting go of worries brings fuller and more meaningful lives.

source_text: Rivers have always played an important role in human life, and learning to navigate them is a skill of great value. Now when I had mastered the language of this water and had come to know every trifling feature that bordered the great river as familiarly as I knew the letters of the alphabet, I had made a valuable acquisition, demonstrating the value of hard-won expertise. But I had fundamentally lost something, too. I had lost something which, it should be noted, could never be restored to me while I lived. All the grace, the beauty, the poetry had gone out of the majestic river! I still keep in mind a certain wonderful sunset which I witnessed when steamboating was new to me. A broad expanse of the river was turned to blood; in the middle distance the red hue brightened into gold, through which a solitary log came floating, black and conspicuous; in one place a long, slanting mark lay sparkling upon the water; in another the surface was broken by boiling, tumbling rings, that were as many-tinted as an opal; where the ruddy flush was faintest, was a smooth spot that was covered with graceful circles and radiating lines, ever so delicately traced; the shore on our left was densely wooded, and the somber shadow that fell from this forest was broken in one place by a long, ruffled trail that shone like silver; and high above the forest wall a clean-stemmed dead tree waved a single leafy bough that glowed like a flame in the unobstructed splendor that was flowing from the sun. There were graceful curves, reflected images, woody heights, soft distances; and over the whole scene, far and near, the dissolving lights drifted steadily, enriching it, every passing moment, with new marvels of coloring. In the end, this experience shows that every gain comes with a loss, and it is a lesson worth carrying with us.
output_text:
I had mastered the language of this water, and every trifling feature along the great river was as familiar to me as the letters of the alphabet. I had gained something valuable. But I had lost something too, something I could never get back as long as I lived. The majestic river had no grace left in it, and no beauty, and no poetry!

One wonderful sunset that I watched when steamboating was new to me has stayed in my mind. A wide stretch of the river had turned to blood. In the middle distance the red brightened to gold, and through the gold floated a solitary log, black and conspicuous. A long, slanting mark sparkled on the water in one place, and in another the surface was broken by boiling, tumbling rings with as many tints as an opal. Where the red flush was faintest lay a smooth patch covered with graceful circles and radiating lines, traced ever so delicately. The shore on our left was thick with woods. The forest cast a somber shadow, and a long, ruffled trail, shining like silver, broke that shadow in one place. High above the wall of forest a dead, clean-stemmed tree waved its one leafy bough, which glowed like a flame in the splendor that flowed unobstructed from the sun. The scene held graceful curves, reflected images, wooded heights, and soft distances. Across the whole of it, far and near, the dissolving lights drifted steadily, and each passing moment they enriched it with new marvels of coloring.
